info.name: 22 · In-app notifications
info.description:
The **in-app notification feed** behind the console bell: read the feed, count what is unread, and mark rows read or unread.

**There is no HTTP create.** Rows are minted only by domain emitters (`create_notification`, which flushes but never commits), so a notice lands **atomically with the transaction that caused it** — a rolled-back verdict announces nothing. This collection therefore has to *earn* its notifications by driving a real emitter rather than posting one.

**The emitter it uses.** The owner creates an evaluation group, the **admin** then moderates it (`request-changes`, later `reject`). Both are group-lifecycle verdicts, and both notify the group's owner. The actor matters: a verdict is **skipped when the actor is the owner** — a self-verdict is not news — which folder A asserts explicitly by having the owner self-approve a second group and produce nothing.

**Flow.** A) mint notifications through the moderation emitters, and prove the self-verdict is silent; B) read the feed — list, filter, unread count, single get; C) mark read / unread, including the "only rows that actually changed" rule and the mark-all form; D) owner-scoping — the feed has **no break-glass**, so not even an admin can read someone else's notification.

**Contract notes.**
- `POST /notifications/mark` returns `{updated: N}` counting **only rows that actually changed state** — re-marking an already-read row returns `updated: 0`. An empty (or omitted) `ids` means *all of the caller's* rows in the opposite state.
- The unread count is `total` on `?read=false` — there is no dedicated count endpoint.
- `object_type` / `object_id` is a **loose pointer** (a validated string, no FK), so the deep-link target may already be gone; the client must tolerate a dangling reference.
- `notifications:read|update` are held by **every** role, like `saved_views:*` — this is personal data, not a privileged view. There is no create or delete member.
- Strictly owner-scoped with **no** break-glass: another user's notification is a **404**.

**Auth model.** Per-request: `{{owner_token}}` is the recipient, `{{admin_token}}` the moderator and the failed snooper. Self-contained apart from the two evaluation groups, which leak (groups have no DELETE route).

**Prereq.** `make seedlocal`.

Verified green on a live stack: 64/64 assertions (Newman).

request.description: The **moderator** — holds `evaluation_groups:manage`, so it can request changes on and reject someone else's group. Also the failed snooper in folder D.
The **recipient** — creates the group whose moderation notifies it.

Only needed because a group create requires a non-empty `allowed_model_ids`. Registered by the admin (`models:create` is admin-only) and referenced by the owner — a group may allow a model its creator cannot manage.

exec: pm.test('the feed is readable by a plain role', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().items).to.be.an('array'));

request.description: `notifications:read` is held by every role. The seeded owner may already carry notifications from an earlier run, so folder A asserts against this **baseline** rather than assuming an empty feed.
**FE note:** the bell's badge is exactly this — `total` on `?read=false`. There is no separate count endpoint.

exec: pm.test('a full create lands as pending_approval', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql('pending_approval'));

request.description: A complete create is submitted for review straight away (`pending_approval`), which is the source state both moderation verdicts need.

`evaluation_groups:manage` — **admin only**, deliberately not the owner-or-manage rule used by approve/publish, so an owner cannot bounce their own group. `changes_requested` is the state the owner can `submit` from again. Takes **no request body** — unlike `reject`, which requires `rejection_reason`.

item.name: 3 · The owner cannot bounce their own group → 403

request.description: The other half of step 2's rule, which was previously only asserted in prose. `request-changes` and `reject` are gated on `evaluation_groups:manage` **alone** — unlike `approve`/`publish`, which follow owner-or-manage — so the group's own owner is refused even on their own group. The gate fires before the state machine, so this is a 403 and not the 409 the current `changes_requested` state would otherwise give.

exec: pm.test('the page really is newest-first', () => pm.expect(ts).to.eql([...ts].sort((x, y) => y - x)));

request.description: The emitter fired inside the verdict's transaction. `object_type` + `object_id` are what the bell deep-links with — a loose pointer, so the client must cope with a target that has since been deleted.

item.name: 5 · The unread badge went up by one

request.description: Asserted as a delta against the Setup baseline, so a seeded owner with pre-existing notices does not make this brittle.

item.name: 6 · Owner creates a second group and approves it themselves

request.description: A second subject, for the self-verdict case.

Approve follows the **owner-or-manage** rule, so an owner may approve their own group (a deliberate decision). Contrast `request-changes` and `reject`, which are manage-only — step 3 proves that with a 403.

**The skip rule.** The emitter is bypassed when the actor *is* the owner — telling someone what they just did themselves is noise. Still `nt_before + 1`, i.e. only folder A step 2's notification exists.

exec: pm.test('the name identifies what emitted it', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().name.toLowerCase()).to.include('change'));

request.description: The detail read the bell uses when a row is expanded.

item.name: 2 · Filter the feed by object type

exec: pm.test('and every row really is of that type', () => pm.expect(items.every(i => i.object_type === 'evaluation_group')).to.eql(true));

request.description: `object_type` accepts `evaluation` or `evaluation_group`. The second assertion checks the filter narrows rather than merely including our row.

exec: pm.test('ascending by created_at', () => pm.expect(ts).to.eql([...ts].sort((a, b) => a - b)));

request.description: `order_by` takes `created_at` or `-created_at` (the default, newest first — what a bell wants).
A well-formed id matching no row of the caller's — indistinguishable from another user's row (folder D), which is the point: the feed leaks no existence.
`notifications:read` is held by every role, but the feed is still per-user, so it is never anonymous.
`notifications:update`. The response counts rows whose state actually flipped.

item.name: 2 · It reads as read, with a timestamp

request.description: `read` is the boolean the UI binds to; `read_at` is when it happened.

item.name: 3 · Marking it read again changes nothing

request.description: **The rule worth pinning.** `updated` is not "rows addressed" but "rows that changed" — the endpoint flips only rows in the *opposite* state. A UI can use the number to decide whether to refresh the badge at all.

item.name: 4 · The unread count is back to the baseline

exec: pm.test('our notification left the unread set', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().total).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get('nt_unread_before'))));

request.description: Closes the loop with folder A step 4: the badge went up by one, and now it is back down.
The flag is a toggle, not a one-way latch — "mark as unread" is a real product action.

exec: pm.test('unread, and the stamp is gone', () => { pm.expect(pm.response.json().read).to.eql(false); pm.expect(pm.response.json().read_at).to.eql(null); });

request.description: Unmarking clears the timestamp, so `read_at` never claims a read that was undone.
An omitted or empty `ids` means **all of the caller's** rows in the opposite state — the bell's "mark all as read". Asserted as *at least* one, because a seeded owner may have had other unread rows.
What "mark all" means, stated as a count.
Idempotent by the same only-real-transitions rule as step 3.

item.name: 1 · Admin cannot read the owner's notification → 404

request.description:
The admin **caused** this notification and still cannot read it. The feed is strictly owner-scoped with **no break-glass** — unlike annotations or flags, where `evaluation_groups:manage` lifts the read scope.

The service documents the reason as the scope itself: notifications are **owner-scoped personal data**, with no admin break-glass and no HTTP create path. For an administrative view of what happened to an object, the audit trail (`17`) is the surface, not someone else's feed.

item.name: 2 · Admin's own feed does not contain it

exec: pm.test('it is not in the moderator\'s feed either', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().items.map(i => i.id)).to.not.include(pm.collectionVariables.get('nt_note_id')));

request.description: The list path is scoped the same way — the moderator sees its own notices only.

exec: pm.test('the foreign id silently matches nothing', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().updated).to.eql(0));

request.description: Marking is scoped too, and an out-of-scope id is simply **not matched** — `updated: 0` rather than a 404, because `mark` is a set operation over the caller's own rows, not an addressed fetch.

exec: pm.test('still read, as the owner left it', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().read).to.eql(true));

request.description: Confirms step 3 changed nothing, checked from the only account that can see the row.

item.name: 1 · Admin rejects the first group → 409 (wrong source state, so nothing is emitted)

exec: pm.test('names the illegal transition', () => { const d = pm.response.json().detail; pm.expect(d).to.include('changes_requested'); pm.expect(d).to.include('not_approved'); });

request.description:
`reject` is the **terminal** moderation verdict (`pending_approval → not_approved`) and records `rejection_reason`.

Asserted as an exact **409**, not a one-of: folder A step 2 moved this group to `changes_requested`, and the only legal source for `reject` is `pending_approval`, so the outcome is deterministic (verified live — `Cannot move evaluation group ... from 'changes_requested' to 'not_approved'`). To see the success path instead, `submit` the group first; the 200 branch is deliberately not asserted here because nothing in this collection can reach it.

Both evaluation groups leak — groups have no DELETE route; `run_suffix` keeps their titles unique. The owner is left with the notifications this run produced, which is what a real feed would look like.
